track.label: Negotiation & Deal-Making
track.summary: Master negotiation from first principles to complex deals — covering BATNA, tactical empathy, salary conversations, vendor contracts, and cross-cultural dynamics so you can consistently reach better agreements.
track.name: negotiation

phases.title: Negotiation Fundamentals
phases.description: Build the conceptual foundation: what negotiation is, why most people do it poorly, the difference between distributive and integrative approaches, and the role of emotion.

phases.title: Preparation & BATNA
phases.description: Learn to prepare systematically — clarify your BATNA, set anchors, research your counterpart's interests, and shift from positions to underlying interests.

phases.title: Tactics & Psychology
phases.description: Study the tactics used by FBI hostage negotiators and experienced deal-makers: tactical empathy, labeling, mirroring, power plays, and cognitive traps to avoid.

phases.title: Salary & Job Offer Negotiation
phases.description: Apply negotiation principles to your own career: salary research, scripted language for the conversation, and navigating total compensation packages.

phases.title: Business Deal Negotiation
phases.description: Negotiate vendor contracts, partnerships, and B2B agreements — including how to close deals and break deadlocks with principled techniques.

phases.title: Cross-Cultural & Complex Negotiations
phases.description: Handle multi-party negotiations, adapt to cultural communication styles, and build the long-term relationships that make future deals easier.

topics.title: Types of Negotiation and Core Concepts
topics.description: Understand negotiation as a structured process, learn the vocabulary — ZOPA, reservation price, value creation vs. claiming — and recognise the most common failure modes.

steps.t: Define ZOPA and reservation price
steps.d: Write down your walkaway price (reservation price) and your counterpart's likely range before your next negotiation, marking the zone of possible agreement between them.

steps.t: Identify failure modes in past deals
steps.d: Review three negotiation outcomes you participated in and write which failure mode sabotaged each: no BATNA, weak anchor, fixed-pie bias, or reactive devaluation.

steps.t: Map positions vs. underlying interests
steps.d: For a current negotiation, list each party's stated position, then underneath write the actual interests driving each position — notice where they differ from the positions.

steps.t: Spot your own common mistake
steps.d: Complete this sentence: 'In negotiations I tend to _____, which costs me _____.' (e.g., anchor too high and damage rapport, or anchor too low and leave money on the table).

steps.t: Prepare vocabulary for your next negotiation
steps.d: Write five phrases you'll actually use: how to name your ZOPA, frame the pie as expandable, ask about their interests, and separate person from problem.

topics.title: Distributive vs. Integrative Bargaining
topics.description: Learn when to use win-lose competitive bargaining and when to pursue integrative deals that expand the pie through trades on differing priorities.

steps.t: Distinguish distributive and integrative trades
steps.d: Using a real deal you know, identify three points where each side wanted different things (time vs. price, volume vs. exclusivity) where integrative trades were possible.

steps.t: Diagram the pie expansion opportunity
steps.d: In a salary negotiation, draw a table showing what employer controls (base salary, bonus, title) vs. what employee controls (start date, remote days, education budget) to find expansion trades.

steps.t: Run one integrative negotiation conversation
steps.d: Conduct an actual conversation where you ask five questions about your counterpart's true priorities before proposing any deal, then propose based on what matters most to them.

steps.t: Measure the difference you created
steps.d: After the conversation, write down the deal you'd have proposed without asking, then the deal you proposed after learning their priorities — quantify the difference.

steps.t: Identify what you left on the table
steps.d: Review the deal that closed and write down one point you now realize both sides valued, but you didn't trade on — mark it for your next negotiation.

topics.title: Psychology and Emotions in Negotiation
topics.description: Explore how anxiety, overconfidence, and reactive devaluation sabotage outcomes — and practical techniques for emotional regulation at the table.

steps.t: Assess your emotional triggers in negotiation
steps.d: List three things your counterpart could say that would anger or frustrate you, then write how you'd physically and verbally respond if you felt that emotion.

steps.t: Build an emotional reset ritual
steps.d: Write a 60-second physical reset (breathe, pause, drink water) that you can use mid-negotiation when frustration or anxiety is rising, then commit to using it in your next call.

steps.t: Separate reactive devaluation from reality
steps.d: After your counterpart makes an offer, write down your immediate gut reaction ('that's offensive'), then force yourself to assess the offer on merit alone, ignoring the emotional sting.

steps.t: Conduct a negotiation while monitoring your state
steps.d: In an actual negotiation, pause three times to notice whether you're anxious, confident, or angry, and write down what triggered each state and whether it affected your decision-making.

steps.t: Adjust your next negotiation for emotion
steps.d: Based on what you learned about your emotional patterns, plan one structural change for your next negotiation (different time of day, different setting, or a break timing) to manage your state better.

topics.title: Understanding and Building Your BATNA
topics.description: Develop a genuine Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement before every negotiation, and learn how improving your BATNA shifts power in your favour.

steps.t: Document your written BATNA
steps.d: Write out your actual best alternative to a negotiated agreement in one paragraph — what you'd do, how long it would take, what it would cost you, not a vague notion.

steps.t: Research your counterpart's BATNA
steps.d: Identify what your counterpart would do if negotiations fail, then estimate how costly or attractive their alternative is compared to a deal with you.

steps.t: Calculate your reservation price in writing
steps.d: Set a hard minimum deal value on paper before you negotiate — the worst acceptable outcome you'd take — and do not move this number based on their pressure during the call.

steps.t: Use BATNA to shape your opening
steps.d: Based on your written BATNA and reservation price, decide whether to open first or let them open, and if you open, anchor above your reservation price by a defensible amount.

steps.t: Verify your BATNA shapes your power
steps.d: Confirm that a strong BATNA (good alternative, high reservation price) makes you more willing to walk away, and that your counterpart senses this in the tone and pacing of your negotiation.

topics.title: Setting Anchors and Opening Offers
topics.description: Study the anchoring effect and learn evidence-backed guidelines for when to open first, how extreme to go, and how to adjust the reference point in your favour.

steps.t: Calculate the anchoring impact on the deal
steps.d: Choose a salary range negotiation, set a high anchor (20% above fair market), a medium anchor (fair market), and a low anchor (20% below fair market), and estimate the settlement point each anchor would create.

steps.t: Practice opening first with supporting logic
steps.d: Make a real opening offer to a counterpart and give them two reasons why your number is justified (market data, time constraints, their stated priorities) to make the anchor less arbitrary.

steps.t: Choose your anchor relative to BATNA
steps.d: Write your opening number and your reservation price on paper; verify the gap between them is defensible if challenged — if your anchor is too extreme, your credibility is shot.

steps.t: Adjust the anchor mid-negotiation if needed
steps.d: After hearing their counter-offer, decide if you misread their BATNA and if your anchor is still optimal; if you adjust, do it as a concession ('I understand now, let me revise to ___') not a retreat.

steps.t: Measure how much the anchor shifted the outcome
steps.d: After closing a deal, calculate how much higher the settlement was than their opening offer, and estimate what your opening anchor caused in that gap.

topics.title: Interest-Based vs. Position-Based Negotiation
topics.description: Move from stated positions to the interests underneath — using the Getting to Yes framework to find creative, durable agreements.

steps.t: Uncover interests beneath stated positions
steps.d: In your next negotiation, ask 'What concerns do you have about this clause?' and 'What would make this feel fair to you?' instead of restating your position when they push back.

steps.t: Reframe the negotiation around shared interests
steps.d: Write down three interests you and your counterpart genuinely share (timely closure, clear terms, sustainable relationship) and open with those before debating positions.

steps.t: Use interest-based language in a proposal
steps.d: Make a proposal that addresses their interests, not just yours — 'I can do X which gives you the certainty you need on Y, in exchange for flexibility on Z that matters to me.'.

steps.t: Identify creative trades on differing priorities
steps.d: Map what each side cares about most and identify one trade where you give on something they care about but you don't, and they give on something you care about but they don't.

steps.t: Validate that your deal is durable
steps.d: After closing an interest-based deal, ask yourself: Would my counterpart recommend this deal to someone similar? If not, you optimized one-off leverage, not underlying interests.

topics.title: Tactical Empathy and the FBI Approach
topics.description: Learn the Chris Voss / Black Swan Group method: tactical empathy, mirroring, labeling, and calibrated questions that lower defences and gather information.

steps.t: Practice tactical empathy in a call
steps.d: In your next negotiation, label one of your counterpart's apparent concerns: 'It sounds like you're worried about execution risk here.' Then ask what specifically worries them.

steps.t: Use mirroring to deepen their response
steps.d: When they finish a statement, repeat the last three words as a question ('...delivery timeline?') and wait five full seconds for them to elaborate instead of moving to your counter-argument.

steps.t: Ask calibrated questions instead of statements
steps.d: Replace 'Here's why your price is too high' with 'How did you land on that price point?' and 'What would have to change for you to move?' to gather information and lower defenses.

steps.t: Diagnose their walkaway point without asking it directly
steps.d: Through calibrated questions, determine what outcome they'd actually accept, what's a face-saving minimum, and where real deadlock lives — not where they say deadlock is.

steps.t: Compare your assumptions before and after tactical empathy
steps.d: Write down what you assumed about their position before you negotiated, then after tactical empathy write what you actually learned about their concerns and priorities — note the gap.

topics.title: Power Tactics and Counter-Tactics
topics.description: Recognise high-pressure tactics — good cop/bad cop, artificial deadlines, bogey — and develop principled counter-moves that maintain the relationship.

steps.t: Identify the power tactic in a past negotiation
steps.d: Recall a negotiation where someone used good cop/bad cop, artificial deadline, or bogey against you; write exactly what they said and how it affected your decision-making.

steps.t: Recognize the tactic being used in real-time
steps.d: In your next negotiation, if your counterpart uses 'My manager won't approve unless you move 10%', pause and write down which hardball tactic that is and what your principled counter-move is.

steps.t: Respond with principle, not capitulation
steps.d: When faced with a power tactic, refuse to move based on the tactic ('I don't negotiate against artificial deadlines') and instead offer to solve the real problem that created the tactic.

steps.t: Maintain the relationship while pushing back
steps.d: After the negotiation, send a message that acknowledges their constraints ('I know your manager had budget limits') while affirming the deal ('Glad we found a solution both sides can own').

steps.t: Plan your counter-move before it happens
steps.d: Before your next high-stakes negotiation, write down which two hardball tactics your counterpart is most likely to use, and write your principled response to each before you get called.

topics.title: Cognitive Biases and Negotiation Traps
topics.description: Identify the most common cognitive biases that distort negotiators — fixed-pie bias, reactive devaluation, escalation of commitment — and how to neutralise them.

steps.t: Spot your fixed-pie bias before the negotiation
steps.d: Write down your opening assumption: 'If they win on X, I must lose on X.' Then identify three points where winning on X could actually help you on Y — break the fixed-pie assumption.

steps.t: Catch reactive devaluation in yourself
steps.d: When your counterpart proposes something you initially liked but now suddenly dislike because *they* proposed it, pause and ask: 'Did the offer actually get worse, or did I just react emotionally?'.

steps.t: Resist escalation of commitment to a position
steps.d: You've said a number publicly; counterpart pushes back hard; write down the sunk cost fallacy temptation ('I've already committed to 10%'), then force yourself to evaluate 8% on its actual merits.

steps.t: Use anchoring to protect against biases
steps.d: Before negotiations, write your anchor and reservation price and your identified biases on a card you keep in front of you during the call to interrupt automatic mental traps.

steps.t: Review a closed deal for cognitive trap traces
steps.d: After closing a deal, write down which cognitive bias (if any) distorted your judgment: Did you see the pie as fixed when it wasn't? Devalue their offer because they made it? Escalate to defend a failed position?.

topics.title: Researching and Setting Your Salary Target
topics.description: Use market data from Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, LinkedIn Salary, and industry surveys to set a defensible target range before any offer conversation.

steps.t: Collect market data from three sources
steps.d: Look up salary data for your role on Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, and LinkedIn Salary; write down the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentile for your location and experience level.

steps.t: Document your personal market value on paper
steps.d: List your relevant skills, years of experience, education, any unique expertise, and how those map to the salary bands you researched — write your defensible target range.

steps.t: Set your negotiation numbers before the offer conversation
steps.d: Write down: opening ask (75th percentile), target (60th percentile), minimum acceptable (50th percentile) — and commit to these numbers before any offer call.

steps.t: Decode the offer package breakdown
steps.d: When you receive an offer, break it into components: base salary, bonus, equity, benefits, and perks — then evaluate each part against your market data and your target.

steps.t: Validate your ask against multiple benchmarks
steps.d: Compare your target salary to industry average, company size/stage benchmarks, and your personal value factors; if your ask contradicts all three, adjust or strengthen your argument.

topics.title: Scripts and Language for Salary Conversations
topics.description: Learn word-for-word scripts for deflecting premature salary questions, responding to an offer, and counter-offering without damaging rapport.

steps.t: Write your deflection script for premature salary questions
steps.d: Before the interview, write word-for-word: 'I'd love to see the full scope first, then we can discuss what's fair.' Practice saying it twice so you can use it naturally.

steps.t: Prepare your response to a lowball offer
steps.d: Write your response in advance: 'Thank you for the offer. I was expecting something closer to [your target] based on market data. Can we work toward that?' — practice delivering it calmly.

steps.t: Craft your counter-offer with supporting logic
steps.d: When you counter, give them two facts that justify your ask: market data from Levels.fyi, and one reason specific to you ('My background in X is rare in this domain').

steps.t: Use silence after your counter to your advantage
steps.d: After you make your counter-offer, stop talking and wait 15 full seconds for them to respond — most people fill silence with concessions, not you.

steps.t: Document the actual offer negotiation on paper
steps.d: Write down their first offer, your counter, their counter-counter, and the final offer in writing — use the recorded history to stay firm on total compensation, not just the salary number.

topics.title: Negotiating Total Compensation and Benefits
topics.description: Go beyond base salary: negotiate equity, signing bonus, remote flexibility, professional development budget, and title — knowing which levers companies move most easily.

steps.t: Identify which non-salary items matter most to you
steps.d: Before any offer negotiation, rank these by personal value: equity, signing bonus, remote days, title, professional development budget, vacation days — put your top three in writing.

steps.t: Research what your target company typically moves on
steps.d: Use Blind and ask contacts at the company: What items are 'locked' (non-negotiable base salary)? What items are 'flexible' (equity, signing bonus)? Note the pattern.

steps.t: Build your total compensation case on their constraints
steps.d: If they won't move base salary, ask 'What flexibility do you have on equity and signing bonus?' — then negotiate those instead of re-litigating base.

steps.t: Negotiate one component to maximize value
steps.d: After settling base salary, move to bonus structure (signing + annual), then equity (amount + vesting), then perks — don't bundle them or you'll lose leverage on the third category.

steps.t: Get the final package in writing before accepting
steps.d: Confirm the offer email includes every component you negotiated: base, signing bonus, equity grant amount and vesting, start date, and any flexibility (remote days, start date, etc.) in writing.

topics.title: Vendor and Contract Negotiation
topics.description: Apply negotiation principles to supplier and vendor relationships — scoping deliverables, SLAs, payment terms, and exit clauses in a way that protects your organisation.

steps.t: Review the contract's scope and deliverables in writing
steps.d: Before negotiating a vendor contract, write down exactly what you expect them to deliver: features, quality standards, timeline — and compare to what's written in their template.

steps.t: Set defensible SLA metrics and consequences
steps.d: For a critical vendor, write down: uptime target (e.g., 99.5%), support response time (2 hours), and penalty if they miss (e.g., monthly credit or service level adjustment).

steps.t: Map your walk-away terms on paper
steps.d: Write down which three contract terms are non-negotiable for you: auto-renewal language, price escalation caps, liability limits — and which ones you can trade away to get those three.

steps.t: Negotiate payment terms and exit clauses
steps.d: Propose payment terms that give you leverage: 30% upfront, 30% at acceptance, 40% at go-live — and write a termination clause that lets you exit with 60 days notice if they fail SLAs.

steps.t: Document the final signed contract against your walk-aways
steps.d: After signing, review the executed contract and verify it includes your three non-negotiable terms, the SLAs you defined, and the payment/exit terms you proposed.

topics.title: Partnership and B2B Deal-Making
topics.description: Structure win-win business partnerships — aligning incentives, sharing risk, building mutual trust, and drafting term sheets that hold up over time.

steps.t: Define mutual value in a term sheet outline
steps.d: Before partnership negotiations, write: What value do we each bring? (access, capability, capital) and what do we each need to win? (revenue, risk-sharing, control) to structure win-win trades.

steps.t: Identify risk-sharing mechanisms for shared upside
steps.d: Propose a deal structure where you both share upside and downside: revenue share (20% to us, 80% to partner) with a guaranteed minimum, or performance milestones tied to payments.

steps.t: Build incentive alignment into the partnership terms
steps.d: Write clause language that ties payments or equity to actual results (revenue targets, product adoption milestones) so you're not paying for effort, you're paying for outcomes.

steps.t: Set governance and decision-making in writing
steps.d: Define how you'll make decisions together: Which decisions require both partners' approval? (strategy, major customers) Which can one partner make alone? (day-to-day operations, hiring).

steps.t: Specify exit scenarios and dispute resolution in advance
steps.d: Write down what happens if: one partner wants out (buyout, forced sale, dissolution), profits diverge from plan (reconciliation process), or you have a strategic disagreement (escalation path to decision).

topics.title: Closing Deals and Breaking Impasses
topics.description: Use principled techniques to move stalled negotiations forward — introducing new variables, using objective criteria, and building post-settlement settlements.

steps.t: Diagnose why the negotiation is stalled
steps.d: Write down the last three offers exchanged and note: Are you stuck on a number? A term? A principle? Naming the actual blockage clarifies what new variable could unstick it.

steps.t: Introduce a new variable to break impasse
steps.d: If price is stuck, propose a new variable: different payment terms, milestone-based pricing, or a pilot program instead of a full rollout — something neither side proposed yet.

steps.t: Propose objective criteria to reset the negotiation
steps.d: Replace 'I want X, you want Y' with 'Industry standard is Z, let's anchor to that.' Use market data, comparable precedents, or third-party benchmarks as the negotiator, not your opinions.

steps.t: Build a post-settlement settlement into the plan
steps.d: Before you reach final agreement, agree to a three-month review: 'We'll revisit this deal after three months of actual performance and adjust if reality diverged from assumptions.'.

steps.t: Document the breakthrough and what unlocked it
steps.d: After reaching agreement, write down: What variable unlocked the deal? Was it price, timing, a new structure, or a principle? Note this for your next stalled negotiation.

topics.title: Cross-Cultural Negotiation Differences
topics.description: Understand how cultural dimensions — individualism, hierarchy, time orientation, and direct vs. indirect communication — shape negotiation norms and expectations.

steps.t: Map cultural dimensions of your counterpart's background
steps.d: Research the communication style (direct vs. indirect), hierarchy expectations (formal vs. informal), time orientation (monochronic vs. polychronic) of their culture before you negotiate.

steps.t: Adjust your pacing and directness to their culture
steps.d: If negotiating with a culture that values indirect communication, avoid blunt ultimatums; instead propose options and let them choose, giving them face-saving room.

steps.t: Recognize different views on relationship vs. task
steps.d: In task-focused cultures, get to business quickly; in relationship-focused cultures, spend time building rapport and trust before negotiating terms — honor the different priority.

steps.t: Prepare for different negotiation taboos
steps.d: Research what's never discussed in their culture (direct conflict, asking about family, discussing profits) and what's always discussed (long-term relationship, stability, fairness) — adapt your language.

steps.t: Confirm your cross-cultural assumptions with them
steps.d: Early in a cross-cultural negotiation, ask: 'What's your preferred communication style?' and 'What's most important to your side in this deal?' — let them tell you rather than assuming.

topics.title: Multi-Party and Team Negotiations
topics.description: Manage coalition dynamics, handle internal misalignment before external negotiations, and coordinate a team at the table to avoid sending mixed signals.

steps.t: Align your team on priorities before the negotiation
steps.d: Before walking into a multi-party negotiation, hold an internal meeting where each team member states their top three priorities and walkaway terms — identify and resolve internal conflicts first.

steps.t: Assign clear roles to each team member
steps.d: Designate: one primary negotiator (does the talking), one listener (takes notes and flags issues), one decision-maker (has veto power) — practice this role clarity in a test negotiation.

steps.t: Establish internal signals for off-table huddles
steps.d: Create a phrase you'll use to call a break if your team disagrees mid-negotiation: 'Let me check with my team' — then huddle privately to realign before responding.

steps.t: Prevent sending mixed signals to the other side
steps.d: In a negotiation with your team, if person A says 'We can do X' and person B says 'Actually, we need Y,' your counterpart will exploit the gap — catch and correct contradictions on the spot.

steps.t: Debrief team performance after the negotiation
steps.d: After closing, have a 20-minute team debrief: What worked? Where were we misaligned? What internal conflicts distracted us? Use this to improve coordination for the next multi-party negotiation.

topics.title: Ethics and Long-Term Relationship Building
topics.description: Distinguish ethical persuasion from manipulation, understand when to walk away, and build the trust-based relationships that produce better deals over time.

steps.t: Distinguish persuasion from manipulation in your tactics
steps.d: Write down a tactic you used in your last negotiation; then ask: Did I give them truthful information? Did I let them make a free choice? If no to either, you crossed into manipulation.

steps.t: Set ethical boundaries before negotiation
steps.d: Before any negotiation, write: I will not lie about X. I will not threaten Y. I will disclose Z if asked. Use this written boundary to resist in-the-moment temptation to overstep.

steps.t: Walk away from unfair deals
steps.d: Identify deal-breakers in advance: bad faith conduct, illegal terms, requests to misrepresent facts — and commit to walking away if any appear, even if the deal is otherwise attractive.

steps.t: Build trust for long-term value over one-deal wins
steps.d: Ask yourself: 'Would I want to negotiate with this person/company again?' If the answer is no, and your tactic is why, you won today's deal but lost future deals and your reputation.

steps.t: Review ethics in closed deals retrospectively
steps.d: After closing a deal you're proud of, ask: Could my counterpart say I was fair? Would they recommend me to others? If you squirm, you chose short-term leverage over long-term relationship.
